steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper analyzing Ethereum's reward system after the Merge. It should give background on Ethereum, explain how block rewards worked under Proof of Work, describe the move to Proof of Stake and the beacon chain, cover what changed in rewards after the Merge, state what our study contributes, and outline the rest of the paper.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Ethereum overview and its incentive program
- Proof of Work era: miners and block proposal
- PoW rewards and the shift to Proof of Stake / beacon chain
- Validator duties and rewards on the beacon chain
- The Merge and the new reward mechanism
- Our contribution
- Paper organization

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Ethereum overview
  - consolidated in Web3/blockchain: decentralized network, more than 5.000 active nodes (cite); multipurpose EVM (cite)
  - pioneer blockchain for Smart Contracts (cite)
  - above 1 million transactions/day, 600 thousand active accounts (cite)
  - relies on an incentive program rewarding honest behavior
- PoW era
  - operative since 2015; PoW consensus
  - miners compete to be next block proposer
  - build block candidates from user transactions in public Mem-pool
  - first valid block -> generous tip in Ether (ETH); iterate nonce values until block hash meets network target
- PoW rewards, move to PoS
  - until EIP1559 (cite): proposers also got transaction fees + dynamically adjusting base reward
  - network resilient, but PoW = huge, unnecessary power consumption
  - one of the biggest upgrades: shift to Proof of Stake (cite)
  - started with side chain only for consensus: Beacon Chain / Consensus Layer (CL)
  - deposit 32 ETH in public smart contract to activate a validator
  - next proposer chosen by randomness generator RANDAO (cite)
  - epochs of 32 slots x 12 seconds = 6.4 minutes; RNG picks proposer each slot
  - no competition -> 99.95% less power; drawback: more complexity for consensus
- Validator duties
  - beacon chain stores validator status: activation, interactions, balance
  - duties every epoch to reach consensus and keep finalization
  - committees vote on correctness of proposed block of their slot -> attestations, included in beacon blocks
  - sync committee: 512 validators sign block headers for light clients
  - rewards for correct duties; honest actions more lucrative than dishonest
- The Merge
  - chains co-existed from December 2020 (beacon chain launch) to September 2022
  - "The Merge" (cite): CL validators also propose blocks on EVM chain = Execution Layer (EL)
  - validators get CL and EL rewards; EL part only transaction fees, no base reward
  - proposers known beforehand, no mining -> more time to include transactions -> more room to gain by filtering/ordering transactions
- Contribution
  - previously unseen approach to measure PoW -> PoS transition in a live network
  - empirical + theoretical methods to score validator duties
  - comparison of reward performance for entities controlling many validators
- Organization: II state of the art; III reward terms, theory, methodology; IV results discussion; V summary

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Ethereum has become well established in the Web3 and blockchain ecosystem. It has a widely decentralized network with more than 5.000 active nodes and a multipurpose Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM). It is often known as the first blockchain that could process Smart Contracts, and today it handles above 1 million transactions per day from 600 thousand active accounts. Like any other blockchain in the Web3 space, Ethereum needs an incentive program that rewards honest behavior between participants in order to support the decentralized platform.

Ethereum started as an operative network in 2015 and it chose Proof of Work (PoW) as its consensus mechanism. In PoW, the participating nodes, which are commonly called miners, competed with each other to be the next block proposer. Nodes built block candidates by adding user transactions from the public Mem-pool. The first miner to publish a valid block got a generous tip in Ethereum's token Ether (ETH), so miners would iterate over many nonce values in parallel until the hash of the whole block satisfied the target required by the network.

Until EIP1559 was applied, block proposers also got the fees from the transactions in the block plus a dynamically adjusting base reward as part of the incentives. The network proved to be resilient, but powering consensus with PoW needed huge and unnecessary amounts of power. So in one of the biggest upgrades of its lifetime, Ethereum started a long journey to move its consensus from PoW to a more sustainable Proof of Stake (PoS). The transition started with launching a side chain whose only purpose was to reach consensus. To participate in this Beacon Chain or Consensus Layer (CL), users have to deposit 32 ETH in a publicly available smart contract to activate a validator. The beacon chain decides the next block proposer (among many other things) with a randomness generator algorithm called RANDAO. The beacon chain is organized in epochs, each epoch has 32 slots of 12 seconds, so an epoch lasts 6.4 minutes. In each slot the RNG algorithm decides which validator can propose the block. Removing the competition between nodes cut the total power consumption of the network by 99.95%, but it added extra complexity to reaching consensus.

- Validator duties
  - beacon chain stores validator status, activation, interactions, balance
  - duties every epoch; committees vote on proposed block -> attestations in beacon blocks
  - sync committee of 512 validators signs headers for light clients
  - rewards make honest actions more lucrative
- The Merge
  - co-existence December 2020 to September 2022; "The Merge"; EL
  - CL + EL rewards, EL only transaction fees, no base reward
  - proposers known beforehand -> more gains from filtering/ordering transactions
- Contribution: new approach to measure PoW -> PoS in live network; empirical + theoretical scoring; comparison of large entities
- Organization: II-V

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Ethereum has become well established in the Web3 and blockchain ecosystem. It has a widely decentralized network with more than 5.000 active nodes and a multipurpose Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM). It is often known as the first blockchain that could process Smart Contracts, and today it handles above 1 million transactions per day from 600 thousand active accounts. Like any other blockchain in the Web3 space, Ethereum needs an incentive program that rewards honest behavior between participants in order to support the decentralized platform.

Ethereum started as an operative network in 2015 and it chose Proof of Work (PoW) as its consensus mechanism. In PoW, the participating nodes, which are commonly called miners, competed with each other to be the next block proposer. Nodes built block candidates by adding user transactions from the public Mem-pool. The first miner to publish a valid block got a generous tip in Ethereum's token Ether (ETH), so miners would iterate over many nonce values in parallel until the hash of the whole block satisfied the target required by the network.

Until EIP1559 was applied, block proposers also got the fees from the transactions in the block plus a dynamically adjusting base reward as part of the incentives. The network proved to be resilient, but powering consensus with PoW needed huge and unnecessary amounts of power. So in one of the biggest upgrades of its lifetime, Ethereum started a long journey to move its consensus from PoW to a more sustainable Proof of Stake (PoS). The transition started with launching a side chain whose only purpose was to reach consensus. To participate in this Beacon Chain or Consensus Layer (CL), users have to deposit 32 ETH in a publicly available smart contract to activate a validator. The beacon chain decides the next block proposer (among many other things) with a randomness generator algorithm called RANDAO. The beacon chain is organized in epochs, each epoch has 32 slots of 12 seconds, so an epoch lasts 6.4 minutes. In each slot the RNG algorithm decides which validator can propose the block. Removing the competition between nodes cut the total power consumption of the network by 99.95%, but it added extra complexity to reaching consensus.

The beacon chain stores all the information about the status of the validators, from when they are activated, to how they interact with the network when they do their duties, and also their balance. To reach consensus and keep the chain finalized, the validators have to do a set of tasks at every epoch. These are also called duties. Validators are grouped in committees, and the main task of a committee is to vote on whether the proposed block (if there is one) of the slot they are assigned to is correct. These votes are called attestations and they are included in the beacon blocks. Validators are also grouped in a sync committee, which is a small set of 512 validators that help sign block headers so that light clients can verify them without syncing the entire chain. Validators get rewarded based on how correctly they do all these duties, as an incentive to behave well in consensus, so honest actions are more economically lucrative than dishonest ones.

The two chains existed in parallel from December 2020, when the beacon chain was launched, until September 2022, when the chain that processes transactions became dependent on the beacon chain for consensus. In this event, called "The Merge", the active validators in the consensus layer also became the ones proposing blocks in the EVM chain (from now on called the Execution Layer (EL)). After the transition from PoW to PoS there are some significant changes in the reward mechanism. Since validators now propose both blocks, they get both the CL and the EL rewards. But from the EL rewards validators only get the part that comes from transaction fees, so there is no base reward anymore. Also, because the block proposers are chosen beforehand and there is no mining process anymore, there is more time to include transactions in a block. This ends up increasing the chances that a proposer gets more rewards by filtering and ordering the transactions.

In this paper we present a previously unseen approach to measure the transition from PoW to PoS in a live-working blockchain network. We use both empirical and theoretical methods to compare and score how well the validators do their duties. We also compare the performance, based on rewards, of entities that represent a large set of validators in the network.

The rest of the paper is organized like this: Section II goes over the state of the art and previous work on the topic, Section III introduces the reward-related terms, the theoretical methods and our methodology, Section IV discusses the results of the study, and Section V summarizes the highlights.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Ethereum [1] has firmly consolidated its place in the Web3 and blockchain ecosystem thanks to its widely decentralized network of more than 5.000 active nodes [2] and its multipurpose Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) [3]. Commonly known as the pioneer blockchain able to process Smart Contracts [4], it currently handles above 1 million transactions per day from 600 thousand active accounts [5]. As with any other blockchain in the Web3 space, Ethereum relies on an incentive program that rewards honest behavior between participants in order to support this decentralized platform.

Starting as an operative network in 2015, Ethereum chose Proof of Work (PoW) as its consensus mechanism. In this PoW-powered platform, participating nodes (commonly known as miners) competed with each other to become the next block proposer. Nodes built block candidates by adding user transactions from the public Mem-pool. Since the first miner to publish a valid block was awarded a generous tip in Ethereum's token Ether (ETH), miners would iterate in parallel over multiple nonce values until the hash of the entire block satisfied the target required by the network.

Initially, as part of the block proposal incentives until EIP1559 [6] was applied, block proposers were also granted the fees from processing the transactions included in the block plus a dynamically adjusting base reward. However, although the network proved to be resilient, powering consensus through PoW required huge and unnecessary power consumption. In one of the biggest upgrades of the platform's lifetime, Ethereum embarked on a long journey to shift its consensus mechanism from PoW to a more sustainable Proof of Stake (PoS) [7]. The transition started with the launch of a side chain with the single purpose of achieving consensus. To participate in this Beacon Chain or Consensus Layer (CL), users now have to deposit 32 ETH in a publicly available smart contract to activate a validator. The beacon chain decides who the next block proposer is (among many other things) using a randomness generator algorithm called RANDAO [8]. The beacon chain is organized in epochs, each containing 32 slots of 12 seconds, so a whole epoch lasts 6.4 minutes. Each slot serves as a time range in which the RNG algorithm decides which validator can propose the block. Removing the competition between nodes to become block proposers reduced the total power consumption of the network by 99.95%, with the significant drawback of adding extra complexity to reaching consensus.

The beacon chain stores all the information on the status of the validators, from when they are activated to their interaction with the network when performing their duties, including their balance. To reach consensus and maintain the finalization of the chain, validators now have to perform a set of tasks, also known as duties, at every epoch. Validators are grouped into committees, whose main task is to vote on the correctness of the proposed block (if any) of the slot they are assigned to. These votes are known as attestations and are included in the beacon blocks. Validators are also grouped into a sync committee, a small set of 512 validators that help sign block headers to prove their validity to light clients that do not need to sync the entire chain. Based on the correctness of all these duties, validators are rewarded as an incentive to behave well in consensus, making honest actions in the network more economically lucrative than dishonest ones.

Both chains co-existed from December 2020, when the beacon chain was launched, until September 2022, when the chain in charge of processing transactions became consensus-dependent on the beacon chain. In this event, called "The Merge" [9], the active validators in the consensus layer also became the ones proposing blocks in the EVM chain (from now on called the Execution Layer (EL)). With the transition from PoW to PoS accomplished, there are some significant changes in the reward mechanism of the platform. Since validators now propose both blocks, they get both the CL and the EL rewards. However, from the EL rewards, validators only earn the part coming from transaction fees, which means there is no base reward anymore. Because block proposers are chosen beforehand and the mining process has been removed, there is more time to include transactions in a block, which ultimately increases the chances of a proposer gaining more rewards by filtering and ordering the transactions.

This paper presents a previously unseen approach to measuring the transition from PoW to PoS in a live-working blockchain network. Our approach uses both empirical and theoretical methods to compare and score how well validators accomplish their duties. Moreover, we compare the reward-based performance of entities that represent a large set of validators in the network.

The paper is organized as follows: Section II introduces the state of the art and previous work on the topic, Section III introduces the reward-related terms, theoretical methods, and the methodology we followed, Section IV discusses the results of the study, and Section V summarizes its highlights.

References:
[1] “Ethereum whitepaper,” https://ethereum.org/en/whitepaper/ .
[2] M. Cortes-Goicoechea and L. Bautista-Gomez, “Discovering the ethereum2 p2p network,” in 2021 Third International Conference on Blockchain Computing and Applications (BCCA) . IEEE, 2021, pp. 81–88.
[3] E. Hildenbrandt, M. Saxena, N. Rodrigues, X. Zhu, P. Daian, D. Guth, B. Moore, D. Park, Y. Zhang, A. Stefanescu et al. , “Kevm: A complete formal semantics of the ethereum virtual machine,” in 2018 IEEE 31st Computer Security Foundations Symposium (CSF) . IEEE, 2018, pp. 204–217.
[4] M. Wohrer and U. Zdun, “Smart contracts: security patterns in the ethereum ecosystem and solidity,” in 2018 International Workshop on Blockchain Oriented Software Engineering (IWBOSE) . IEEE, 2018, pp. 2–8.
[5] P. H. F. Oliveira, D. M. Rezende, H. S. Bernardino, S. M. Villela, and A. B. Vieira, “Analysis of account behaviors in ethereum during an economic impact event,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2206.11846 , 2022.
[6] T. Roughgarden, “Transaction fee mechanism design for the ethereum blockchain: An economic analysis of eip-1559,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2012.00854 , 2020.
[7] F. Saleh, “Blockchain without waste: Proof-of-stake,” The Review of financial studies , vol. 34, no. 3, pp. 1156–1190, 2021.
